consideration of above materials on record the Judges of the Courts 
below have concurrently found that the plaintiff did not have any 
lawful title and possession in the disputed land and in the absence of 
any claim of misreading or non-consideration of any evidence on record 
this Court cannot interfere with above concurrent findings of fact. The 
learned Joint District Judge has rightly on correct appreciation of 
materials on record dismissed the appeal which calls for no 
interference.  
I have considered the submissions of learned Advocate for 
opposite party No.1 and carefully examined all materials on record 
including the pleadings, judgments of the Courts below and evidence 
on record. 
It is admitted that plot No.440 comprising 11 decimals land was 
recorded in C.S. Khatian No.320 in the names of the predecessors of the 
plaintiff Monai Mattabar and others and 4 decimals land of above plot 
was subsequently acquired by the Government. It is also admitted that 
disputed 7 decimals land of above plot has been recorded in the name

signboard.

Khatian that in the relevant column of the possession  clear mention has 
been made that by way of exchange Afil Uddin, predecessor of 
defendant No.1 is in possession in 11 decimals land of disputed plot 
No.440.

claim that above entry in the C.S. Khatian was erroneous nor the 
plaintiff sought any relief against above entry in the disputed C.S. 
Khatian. There is no evidence on record to hold that above entry as to 
possession of the disputed land as made in the C.S. Kuatian was 
erroneous or fraudulent which did not represent the correct position of 
the disputed land. The source of claim of title of the plaintiff is above 
C.S. Khatian and above entry in the C.S. Khatian shows that the claim 
of title of the plaintiff does not have any legal basis at all.  
Chand Miah the father of the defendant has claimed to have 
purchased disputed land from heirs of above Afil Uddin by a registered 
kabala deed dated 18.11.1957 and he transferred above land to

explanation: The Court observed that the plaintiff rested her title on the C.S. khatian, and that the same khatian, in its possession column, recorded that the defendant's predecessor had been in possession of the whole plot by way of exchange. appeal for hearing on 02.05.2024.

above case a warrant of arrest was issued against the petitioner. The 
learned District Judge granted bail to the petitioner till 02.05.2024 and 
directed him to deposit the outstanding decreetal money vide 
impugned order dated 16.04.2024.

learned District Judge above appellant as petitioner moved to this 
Court and obtained this Rule.

submits that the learned District Judge registered the appeal but did not 
dispose of the same on merit. By preferring above appeal the petitioner 
has challenged the legality and propriety of the impugned judgment 
and decree. But the learned District Judge has most illegally directed 
the petitioner to deposit full decreetal amount of money before disposal 
of the appeal which is not tenable in law.

input_summary: The PETITIONER, the defendant and appellant in a family appeal, obtained a Rule under section 115(1) of the Code of Civil Procedure against order No.5 dated 16.04.2024 of the District Judge in that appeal, which arose out of the Family Court's judgment and decree dated 30.10.2023 on the OPPOSITE PARTY's suit for dower and maintenance. The PETITIONER preferred an appeal after a delay of fourteen days and applied under section 5 of the Limitation Act, 1908 for the delay to be condoned; the District Judge kept that application to be heard along with the appeal on its merits, registered the appeal without admitting it, gave bail in the execution proceedings and directed the PETITIONER to deposit the outstanding decretal money. explanation: The Court held that the District Judge had proceeded irregularly: a petition for condonation of delay has to be heard and decided first, and only if the delay is condoned can the appeal be admitted, so keeping that petition for hearing along with the appeal on its merits could not be sustained. It further observed that the appeal had been registered without being admitted, and that requiring the appellant to deposit the entire outstanding decretal amount before the appeal was heard would defeat the purpose of appealing at all. Setting that order aside, it directed that the condonation petition be taken up, and the appeal heard on merit expeditiously if delay were condoned.

input_summary: The PETITIONERS, the defendants in a partition suit who had appealed against a preliminary decree, obtained a Rule under section 115(1) of the Code of Civil Procedure against the judgment and decree of the Additional District Judge in an other class appeal concerning the trial court's decree in that suit. The OPPOSITE PARTIES, as plaintiffs, had sued for a declaration that an auction sale held in execution of a rent decree was unlawful and not binding on them, and for partition, claiming title through purchases from the heirs of the original recorded tenants. The PETITIONERS asserted that the disputed holding was sold at auction in execution of that rent decree, that they bought it and have held it since, raising a dwelling house and digging a pond. The preliminary decree went in the plaintiffs' favour.
explanation: The Court observed that the pleadings showed each side denying that the other had any right, title or possession, and neither accepting the other as a co-sharer. It held that a partition suit lies only between co-sharers, that the relief of partition was the substance of the suit while the declaration against the auction sale was ancillary, and that a plaintiff who does not accept the defendant as a co-sharer cannot sue for partition. It further found that an earlier suit for declaration and possession over part of the same land had gone against the plaintiffs' predecessor on title, that no appeal was taken, and that the present suit was barred by res judicata under section 11 of the Code.

The suit sought to restrain the OPPOSITE PARTY, widow of a deceased kinsman, from transferring two scheduled properties while it was pending; the trial court restrained her as to both, the appellate court only as to the first schedule. Before this Court the PETITIONERS submitted that a widow's power of transfer for legal necessity cannot be restrained, that no transfer had yet taken place so the suit was premature and the plaint open to challenge, and that the second property, conveyed in the deceased's name alone, was bought from joint family funds.
explanation: The Court held that under the customary Hindu law a widow takes her husband's property as a limited interest holder with a power of transfer for legal necessity, and that a court cannot deny that power; the reversioners acquire a right to claim title or possession only on her death, and can question a transfer for want of legal necessity only then. Since no transfer had taken place, a restraint on her was not warranted, and an interim order could not be used to give the relief sought in the main suit. The claim that the second property was bought from joint funds could not be resolved in a suit for perpetual injunction.

Their suit sought a declaration that classifying their accounts as defaulted, designating them as defaulting borrowers and sending their names to the central bank's credit information bureau for publication were unlawful, and they sought an interim restraint. The application for an interim restraint against further classification, circulation and publication of their status was declined by the Joint District Judge. explanation: The Court held that the relationship between the parties arises out of a syndicated loan agreement and is contractual, and that in a contractual dispute a temporary injunction is not a just, equitable and appropriate remedy; by the application the petitioners were in effect seeking the relief of the main suit without proving their case at trial. The application was therefore barred.

input_summary: The PETITIONER, the plaintiff in a partition suit, obtained a Rule under section 115(1) of the Code of Civil Procedure against the judgment and decree of the District Judge in a partition appeal concerning the trial court's preliminary and final decrees in that suit. The trial court had passed a preliminary decree giving the PETITIONER a separate share of the land claimed and, on the Commissioner's report, made it final; the defendants had not sought a share of their own. On the defendants' appeal the District Judge displaced that report and the final decree and ordered a fresh investigation, taking the view that the defendants wished to move their dwelling house to the front of the paved road while the PETITIONER's house already stood there. Before this Court the PETITIONER contended that the existing possession resulted from an amicable partition and could not be disturbed for the defendants' convenience.
explanation: The Court held that the object of a partition suit is to divide joint property by metes and bounds according to the shares, and that while doing so a court must not disturb an existing possession which was acquired amicably and does not exceed the co-sharer's lawful share. Partition through court, it observed, does not provide for relocating a co-sharer's settled possession by demolishing houses or cutting standing trees merely because the previous arrangement has become inconvenient for one party. No defect had been alleged against the Commissioner's report, and no case was made that the plaintiffs held more than their share. The trial court's decrees were therefore restored.

input_summary: The PETITIONER, the plaintiff in a suit for declaration of title over a stated area of land, applied to the High Court Division in a civil revision seeking leave to withdraw the suit for a formal defect with liberty to bring a fresh one. He explained that his advocate, through inexperience, had failed to set out the chain of title in the schedule to the plaint, so that the averments and the schedule did not convey a coherent picture and the real controversy could not be adjudicated; he maintained that the defect could not be cured by amendment, that he stood to suffer irreparable loss for no fault of his own, and that he was willing to pay costs to the contesting defendants. explanation: The Court examined the application and found little substance in it, observing that the plaintiff had come forward only after being unsuccessful in the courts below. It nevertheless took note of the explanation that the plaint had been drafted defectively by the advocate and that the schedule did not convey the true position of the land, and of the applicant's offer to pay costs. In the particular circumstances it permitted the withdrawal with liberty to bring a fresh suit on the same cause of action, subject to a condition: if a fresh suit were brought, the plaintiff was to deposit a stated sum in court for the contesting defendants, who could withdraw it.

input_summary: The PETITIONER, the plaintiff in a suit for declaration of title, obtained a Rule under section 115(1) of the Code of Civil Procedure against the judgment and order of the District Judge in a title appeal by which the appeal was dealt with summarily on the ground of limitation, the trial court's decree in the suit standing in the way. The appeal had been presented with an application to excuse a delay of a considerable number of days. Before this Court the PETITIONER contended that the delay had been properly explained and that the appeal ought to have been heard on its merits. The OPPOSITE PARTIES maintained that the reasons given for the delay were vague and unspecific, that the record of rights stands in the names of the defendants' predecessors, and that a defence witness had admitted the defendants' possession.
explanation: The Court scrutinised the application for excusing the delay and found the grounds stated in it to be vague and unsatisfactory, and concluded that the plaintiffs had been grossly negligent in preparing and moving the appeal. It also noted the deposition of a defence witness, which showed the defendants to be in possession of the suit land, and observed that the trial court had considered the material points and found that the plaintiffs had not established right, title or possession. Finding no flaw in the reasoning of the appellate court, it held that the Rule must fail.

input_summary: The PETITIONER, a defendant in a suit for registration of a deed of sale, obtained a Rule under section 115(1) of the Code of Civil Procedure against the judgment and decree of the Special District Judge in a title appeal concerning the trial court's decree in that suit. The OPPOSITE PARTY, as plaintiff, asserted that he had agreed to buy land from his sister for a stated consideration, that she executed a deed after reading it out and receiving the money, that registration could not be completed that day for want of stamp fees, and that she later declined to register it, so he sought registration through the court. The defendants asserted that the same land had earlier been sold to them by registered conveyances, that the plaintiff's deed was created collusively and is not genuine, and that the suit is barred by the law of registration.
explanation: The Court analysed the evidence of the five witnesses produced by the plaintiff, including the deed writer, and found that they spoke with one voice about payment of the consideration and execution of the deed, and that nothing had been elicited in cross-examination to displace them. It held that the suit, brought in time, was not affected by the provisions of the law of registration on which the defendants relied, since those provisions govern an agreement for sale rather than a sale deed executed by the owner. The question of maintainability had been raised for the first time in revision and turned on evidence. The concurrent decrees were left standing.

input_summary: The PETITIONER, the defendant in a partition suit, obtained a Rule under section 115(1) of the Code of Civil Procedure against the judgment and order of the Joint District Judge in a title appeal by which the appellate court sent the suit back for a fresh trial, the trial court having earlier decided against the plaintiffs. The OPPOSITE PARTIES had sued for partition of the scheduled land; the PETITIONER contested, denying the averments and pleading that the suit was not maintainable in its present form and manner and was bad for defect of parties. Before this Court the PETITIONER contended that the appellate court, being empowered to take evidence and to decide the appeal itself, had shirked its responsibility by remitting the case. The OPPOSITE PARTIES' advocate conceded that such a direction to the appellate court would be acceptable.
explanation: The Court held that the appellate court, being empowered under section 107 of the Code read with Order 41 Rule XXIII to take evidence and decide the case itself, ought not to have remitted the suit for retrial, and that in doing so it had avoided deciding the appeal. It observed that the appellate court had itself recorded that the suit was defective for want of parties, barred by limitation and not maintainable without a declaration, yet had not proceeded to decide on those grounds. Both sides having agreed that further evidence could be taken, the case was sent back to the appellate court rather than the trial court for a proper judgment.

input_summary: The PETITIONER, the defendant in a partition suit, obtained a Rule under section 115(1) of the Code of Civil Procedure against the judgment and decree of the District Judge in a title appeal concerning the trial court's decree in that suit. The OPPOSITE PARTIES, as plaintiffs, had sued for partition of the scheduled land; the defendants denied the averments and pleaded that a partition suit unaccompanied by a prayer for declaration of title is not maintainable. The trial court decreed the suit and the appellate court took the same view. At the hearing of the Rule the OPPOSITE PARTIES applied for the Rule to be dealt with on the ground that a final decree had since been passed after acceptance of the Commissioner's report, and that no revisional application lies against a final decree. The PETITIONER's advocate could not meet that contention and left the matter to the Court.
explanation: The Court examined the certified copy of the order by which the final decree was passed and found that, after accepting the Commissioner's report, the trial court had passed the final decree before the revision was brought. Following the precedent relied on, it held that once the report is confirmed or varied the court is obliged to pass a final decree, and that thereafter no revisional application lies: the remedy is an appeal, in which the objections taken to the report may be raised. On that view the revision was incompetent and could not be maintained, and the order of stay operated to protect the petitioner on limitation.

cross-examination that he did not see the recovery of the money. He 
saw that the money was kept on the table. P.W. 12 Magistrate Tasim-
Al-Yeasin affirmed that he saw the money on the table and that at the 
time of recording the statement to the police, it was instructed that the 
money was recovered from the drawer of the accused. P.W. 3 Serajul 
Haque is the Assistant Director, Anti-corruption Commission. He 
stated that as a member of the trap team on 13.7.2014, he went to the 
office of the Taxes Circle-75, Taxes Zone-4 and took position on the 
3rd floor and at that time Assistant Commissioner Maksud (PW-5) was 
present along with him. The above evidence of the prosecution 
witness depicts that there is a contradiction in the evidence of P.Ws. 

<<PAGE 20>>
20 
ABO Hasan 
 
11, 5, 6 and 12 as regards the handing over bribe and recovery of Tk. 
20000 from the drawer of the table of the accused.  
On scrutiny of the above evidence of the prosecution 
witnesses, it reveals that the P.W.11 Abul Kashem Bhuiyan allegedly 
handed over Tk. 20,000 to the accused Md. Zahed Iqbal Khan. During 
cross-examination, P.W. 11 stated that at the time of the handover of 
the bribe, the constables of the ACC were present and within one 
minute, the Magistrate (P.W.12), Deputy Director Abu Sayed 
(P.W.2), Director Abdul Aziz (not examined) along with 4/5 other 
persons entered the room. P.Ws 4 and 5 stated that they were not 
present at the time of handing over the bribe. Subsequently, they went 
to the 5th floor and saw that the accused was detained along with the 
money. P.W.12 stated that the money was recovered from the drawer 
of the accused. During cross-examination, he stated that he saw that 
the money was kept on the table of the accused. From the evidence of 
P.W. 11, it is clear as daylight that the Magistrate(P.W.12), Deputy 
Director Abu Sayed(P.W.2), and Director Abdul Aziz (not examined) 
entered the room of accused Md. Zahed Iqbal Khan at the same time. 
P.W. 12 Magistrate Tasim Al Yeasin did not corroborate the evidence 
of P.Ws. 1, 2 and 4 that the money was recovered from the drawer of 
the accused in his presence. The evidence of P.W.11 that at the time 
of handing over the bribe to the accused, constables of ACC were also 
present there is not corroborated by P.Ws. 5 and 6 who are the 
constables of ACC. If the Magistrate (P.W.12) entered the room of the 
accused along with P.Ws. 2, 5 and 6 there is no scope to witness the 
different facts. Admittedly P.W. 12 Magistrate Tasim Al-Yeasin and 
P.W. 2 Deputy Director Abu Sayed entered the room of the accused at 
the same time, but evidence of P.W. 2 regarding the recovery of the 
money from the middle drawer of the accused is contradicted by P.W. 
12. 

<<PAGE 21>>
21 
ABO Hasan 
 
In view of the above evidence, I am of the view that the alleged 
money was recovered from the table of the accused, not from the 
middle drawer of the table used by accused Md. Zahed Iqbal Khan. 
Keeping money on the table of the accused by P.W. 11 Abul Kashem 
Bhuiyan does not mean that the accused accepted the bribe unless the 
accused received the money and kept it in his drawer or in his pocket. 
P.W. 12 stated that at the time of recording his statement by police, it 
was instructed that money was recovered from the drawer of the 
accused. The above evidence of P.W. 12 depicts that the money 
recovered from the middle drawer of the accused is a subsequent 
embellishment and afterthought. 
 P.W. 14 Shafiqul Islam is a Data Entry Control Operator of 
ACC. He stated that on 13.7.2014 he along with Abul Kashem 
Bhuiyna went to the Office of the accused Zahed Iqbal Khan and in 
his presence, P.W. 11 Abul Kashem Bhuiyan handed over Tk. 20,000 
to the accused as a bribe. The above evidence of P.W. 14 is not 
corroborated by P.W.11.  P.W. 14 Shafiqul Islam is not a member of 
the trap team. There was no reason for P.W 14 to go to the officer of 
the accused. None of the P.W stated that P.W. 14 Shafiqul Islam also 
went along with them. I am of the view that the P.Ws. 14 Shafiqul 
Islam is a chance witness. Therefore, the evidence of P.W. 14 cannot 
be relied on by this court to find the accused guilty of the offence 
under section 161 of the Penal Code,1860 and section 5(2) of the 
Prevention of Corruption Act, 1947. 
In view of the evidence, facts and circumstances of the case 
and the findings, observation and proposition, I am of the view that 
the prosecution failed to prove the charge against the accused beyond 
all reasonable doubt. The trial court without proper assessment and 

<<PAGE 22>>
22 
ABO Hasan 
 
evaluation of the evidence of the prosecution witnesses illegally 
recorded the finding of guilt of the accused. 
I find merit in the appeal.  
Accordingly, the appeal is allowed. 
The impugned judgment and order of conviction and sentence 
passed by the trial court against the accused Md. Zahed Iqbal Khan is 
hereby set aside. 
Send down the lower Court’s record at once.
input_summary: The APPELLANT, a government tax office employee, challenged in a criminal appeal his conviction and sentence for taking a bribe, recorded by the Divisional Special Judge in a special case arising out of a police case initiated on a complaint to the anti-corruption commission. The complainant had alleged that he had already paid a sum to have an error in an income tax return corrected, that the APPELLANT then demanded a further sum to issue the demand note, and that a recorded conversation led him to approach the commission. A trap was arranged with a magistrate and independent witnesses; currency notes were inventoried and handed over, and the money was said to have been recovered from the drawer of the APPELLANT's table. He was convicted under the Penal Code and the anti-corruption law and sentenced to imprisonment and fine.
explanation: The Court found material contradictions among the prosecution witnesses on the central fact. The complainant said the money passed in the constables' presence and that the magistrate, a deputy director and the supervising director entered together, yet the constables said they did not see the recovery, and the magistrate said the money was lying on the table rather than in the drawer, adding that he was told what to record. The Court held that money left on the table does not show acceptance of a bribe, and that the drawer account was an afterthought. An official who claimed to have witnessed the handing over was a chance witness, and the charge was not proved beyond reasonable doubt.

The prosecution case, in short, is that plots No. 15, 16, 19, 24 
and 28 under Shitalakhsa mouza of the then Narayongonj Thana 
originally belonged to the M/S. Raj Brothers Limited and the said

Subsequently, the Jute Trading Corporation was abolished and

Trading Corporation were handed over to the Bangladesh Jute 

<<PAGE 3>>
3 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 
Corporation. The said property was leased out on 05.11.1977 to 
M/S. Momtaz Jute Belling Ltd. Subsequently, in the meeting dated 
28.03.1981 of the Jute Trading Corporation (JTC) a decision was 
taken to sell Plot No. 15 and 19 and notice was published on 
18.04.1981 in the Daily Ittefaq and the Daily Observer under the 
signature of the accused Md. Maij Uddin, Secretary of the Jute 
Trading Corporation. The M/S. Mamtaz Jute Belling Company 
became the highest bidder and agreed to purchase the plots at a price 
of Tk. 12,75,000. Subsequently, it was found that in the tender 
submitted by Mamtaz Uddin, additional Plot No. 24 was also 
included. The accused Maij Uddin and Lutfar Rahman in connivance 
with each other in a meeting dated 13.06.1981 of the Jute Trading 
Corporation decided to sell the holding Nos. 15, 19 and 24  at price 
of Tk. 12,75,000 and directed the accused Mamtaz Belling to deposit 
the money. After depositing the money, the accused Lutfar Rahman 
by order dated 01.09.1984 directed the accused Abul Hossain. 
Inspector of JTC to hand over the possession of holding Nos. 15, 19 
and 24. The accused Abul Hossain submitted the report on 
29.06.1986 to hand over plots Nos. 15, 19, and 24 along with plots 
Nos. 16 and 28, total 1.455 acres of land to Ms Mamataj Belling 
Company Ltd. The accused Mamtaz Uddin is the owner of the 
Mamtaz  Belling Ltd. The accused Abdul Motaleb, Office Assistant 
and Deputy Secretary Imamul Mohit made a recommendation on 
10.11.1990 to hand over 5 plots and send the file to the legal advisor. 
The accused Nuruzzaman Khan, Additional Secretary of the JTC, 
was entrusted with the registration of the deed in favour of the 
purchaser Mamtaz Belling Limited and accordingly, he executed 
deed No. 1657 dated 21.5.1991 in favour of Mamtaz Belling Ltd 
transferring the plot Nos. 15, 16, 19, 24 and 28. The accused persons 

<<PAGE 4>>
4 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 
in connivance with the accused Mamtaz Hossen, owner of Ms. 
Mamtaz Belling Ltd, transferred the additional 1.155 acres of land 
valued at Tk. 49,08,750.  
The informant Md. Musleh Uddin was appointed as the 
investigating officer of the case by the Bureau of Anti-Corruption. 
During investigation, the investigating officer seized the alamats, 
recorded the statement of witnesses under section 161 of the Code of 
Criminal Procedure, 1898 and after completing investigation, he 
found prima facie truth of the allegation made against the accused 
Maij Uddin, Lutfar Rahman, Enamul Muhit, Abul Hossein 
Chowdhury 
and 
submitted 
charge 
sheet 
under

420/409/467/468/471/109 of the Penal Code, 1860 read with section 
5(2) of the Prevention of Corruption Act, 1947. After that, the Chief 
Metropolitan Magistrate, Dhaka sent the case to the Metropolitan 
Sessions Judge, Dhaka.  
The Metropolitan Senior Special Judge, Dhaka took 
cognizance of the offence against the accused persons under sections 
409/420/467/468/471/109 of the Penal Code, 1860 read with section 
5(2) of the Prevention of Corruption Act, 1947 and send the case to 
the Divisional Special Judge, Dhaka who framed charge against the 
accused persons under sections 409/420/467/468/471/109 of the 
Penal Code, 1860 read with section 5(2) of the Prevention of 
Corruption Act, 1947 which was read over and explained to the 
accused persons except accused Samsuddin Ahmed who was 
absconding. The prosecution examined 4 witnesses to prove the 
charge against the accused persons and the defence cross-examined 
P.Ws 2 and 3 and declined to cross-examine P.Ws. 1 and 4. After 
examination of the prosecution witnesses, the accused persons 

<<PAGE 5>>
5 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 
present in court were examined under section 342 of the Code of 
Criminal Procedure, 1898 and they declined to adduce any D.W.  
P.W. 1 Colonel Shariful Islam (Rtd.) is the Chairman of BJC, 
Dhaka. He stated that he is a patient with Parkinson's disease and he 
lost his memory. He could not remember anything about the 
occurrence. He submitted a medical certificate. The defence declined 
to cross-examine P.W. 1. 
P.W.2 Khaza Ahmed Talukder stated that from 10.5.1977 to 
31.12.2002 he was the Executive Engineer of the Bangladesh Jute 
Corporation. In 1981, the authority instructed him to prepare the 
valuation of the assets of the Raj Brothers and accordingly, he 
submitted the report. A decision was taken to sell the assets of Raj 
Brothers by tender. He was a member of the tender opening 
committee. After opening the tender, he sent a report to the 
concerned department. During cross-examination, he stated that he 
prepared the valuation report. He could not say whether he prepared 
the report for the entire property of Raj Brother Estate. He denied the 
suggestion that he was not a member of the tender opening 
committee. He stated that he could not remember when he made 
statement to the investigating officer. During cross-examination on 
behalf of accused Abul Hossain Chowdhury and Abdul Motaleb, he 
stated that he was not aware of the allegation made against the

P.W. 3 Kamrul Islam is the Head Assistant(Rtd.) of 
Bangladesh Betar, Agargaon, Dhaka. He stated that in 1994 when he 
was on deputation with Jute Corporation as Assistant, Inspector Md. 
Lutfar Rahman seized the documents from Secretary Abdur Rab. He 
proved the seizure list as exhibit-1 and his signature on the seizure

list as exhibit-1/1 and handed over the documents to the Secretary. 
He proved the alamats as exhibit-2 series. During cross-examination, 
he stated that he was not aware of the occurrence and seized 
documents.  
P.W. 4 Belayet Hossen is the ASP, RAB-3, Dhaka. He stated 
that on 20.05.1995 he was posted as S.I. at Ramna Thana. On that 
day, he received the FIR from Muslim Uddin, Inspector of the 
Bureau of Anti-Corruption, and filled up the FIR form and lodged 
the FIR. He proved the FIR as exhibit-3 and his signature as exhibit-
3/1. He filled up the FIR form as exhibit-3/Ka and his signature as 
exhibit-3Ka/1. The defence declined to cross-examine P.W.4. 
The learned Advocate Mr Muklesur Rahman having filed an 
affidavit sworn on 19.05.2024 by Ferzana Akter Mukta, niece of the 
appellant Maij Uddin, annexed a death certificate issued by 
Kingstone Hospital, Pallabi, Dhaka, a certificate issued from the 
Rayerbazar Graveyard, Dhaka North City Corporation and the death 
certificate dated 14.07.2020 issued by Councilor Md. Humayun 
Rashid, Dhaka North City Corporation stating that the appellant 
Maij Uddin died on 07.07.2020 due to illness and was buried at

the Secretary of Jute Corporation and the decision was taken by the 
Jute Corporation to sell the property to the highest bidder M/S. 
Mamtaz Belling Ltd and as per the decision of the Bangladesh Jute 
Corporation as members Secretary, the appellant only discharged his 
official duty following the decision taken by the Bangladesh Jute 
Corporation and the prosecution failed to prove the charge against 
the accused beyond all reasonable doubt. Therefore, he prayed for

<<PAGE 7>>

The learned Advocate Mr Mokhlesure Rahman appearing on 
behalf of the appellants Enamul Muhit and Abul Hossein 
Chowdhury submits that following the decision of the Board of the 
Jute Corporation and the instruction of the then Secretary Maij 
Uddin, the appellants only handed over the possession of the 
disputed plots following the sale deed. He further submits that the 
informant and the investigating officer were not examined in the 
case and the prosecution only examined 4 witnesses out of 10 
witnesses cited in the charge sheet and due to non-examination of 
the material witnesses defence was seriously prejudiced. He then 
submits that none of the prosecution witnesses mentioned the name 
of the appellants and the prosecution failed to prove the charge 
against the appellants beyond all reasonable doubt. Therefore, he 
prayed for allowing the appeal.  
The learned Advocate Mr. Md. Omar Farook appearing on 
behalf of respondent No. 2 ACC in both the appeals submits that the 
accused Maij Uddin, Secretary of BJC, published a tender in the 
Daily Ittefaq and the Daily Observer to sell the holding Nos. 15 and 
19 under Shitalakhsa mouza belonged to the BJC and accused 
persons in connivance with the highest bidder Mamtaz Uddin 
tempering the tender notice inserted plot No. 24 in the tender. 
Subsequently, suppressing the original tender notice in connivance 
with said Mamtaz Uddin obtained the order from the Board to sell 
Plot Nos. 15, 19 and 24. The accused persons mala fide to 
misappropriate the property of the BJC included the plot Nos. 16 and 
28 in the deed and illegally transferred the holding Nos. 16, 24 and 
28 along with holding Nos. 15 and 19. Thereby committed offence 
under sections 409/468 of the Penal Code, 1860 read with section

8 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 
5(2) of the Prevention of Corruption Act, 1947. He prayed for the

I have considered the submission of the learned Advocate Mr. 
Mukhlesur Rahman who appeared on behalf of the appellants and 
the learned Advocate Mr. Omar Farook who appeared on behalf of 
respondent No. 2 ACC in both the appeals and perused the evidence, 
impugned judgment and order passed by the court below and the 
records.  
At the very outset, it is noted that the learned Advocate Mr 
Mukseshur Rahman having filed an affidavit sworn on 19.05.2024 
by one Farzana Akter Mukta, niece of the appellant Maij Uddin, 
annexed a death certificate issued by the Kingstone Hospital Ltd, 
Dhaka, a certificate issued by the Rayer Bazar Graveyard and a 
death certificate issued by Councilor Md. Humayun Rashid, Dhaka 
North City Corporation as annexure-x,x1 and x2 stating that during 
the pendency of the appeal, the appellant Maij Uddin died on 
07.07.2000 due to his illness. No one raised any objection against 
the said affidavit. Since the appellant Maij Uddin died during the 
pendency of the appeal, I am of the view that the impugned 
judgment and order of conviction passed against the accused Maij 
Uddin is abated because of the provision made in section 431 of the 
Code of Criminal Procedure, 1898 and the sentence of fine imposed 
by the trial court against him is required to be disposed of 
considering the merit of the case.  
On perusal of the records, it appears that the holding Nos. 15, 
16, 19, 24, and 28 under Shitalakhsa Mouza, Narayangonj belonged 
to Bangladesh Jute Corporation Limited. During the trial of the case, 
P.W. 3 Md. Kamrul Islam proved all the documents relating to the 

<<PAGE 9>>
9 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 
sale and handing over possession of the said plots as exhibit-2 series. 
The accused Maij Uddin, Secretary of the Bangladesh Jute 
Corporation Limited, published a tender notice on 18.04.1981 to sell 
the holding Nos. 15 and 19. Tempering the schedule of the said 
tender notice by different ink and handwriting inserted holding No. 
24 in the records.  
On perusal of the comparative statement of tender No. 
DS/JTC/J/Disposal-2/18-81/1152 reveals that after writing the 
holding Nos. 15 and 19, holding No. 24 was inserted by retyping 
‘24’ below the holding Nos. 15 and 19. The accused Md. Maij Uddin 
as Secretary of BJC by Memo No. DS/JTC/Disposal-2/80-81/259(3) 
dated 21.05.1981 instructed the Mamtaz Jute Belling Company to 
deposit the tender value of the holding No. 15,19 and 24 accepting 
the tender of the highest bidder Mamtaz Jute  Belling Ltd.  
In the 60th meeting of the Board of Directors of Jute Trading 
Corporation Limited held on 13.06.1981 a decision was taken to sell 
plots No. 15 19 and 24 and accused Maij Uddin was discharging his 
duty as Secretary of the Board which decided to sell the said three 
plots. After decision dated 13.06.1981, Deed No. 1657 dated 
21.05.1991 was executed by the Bangladesh Jute Corporation Ltd 
inserting plot Nos. 15, 16, 19, 24 and 28, Sultan Gish Uddin Road, 
under Shitalakhsa Mouza, Narayangonj in the schedule. Before 
registration of the said deed, the accused Abul Hossen by letter dated 
29.06.1985 written to the Deputy Secretary, Jute Trading 
Corporation, Head Office affirmed that as per direction and 
advertising of the Deputy Secretary, Jute Corporation Ltd contained 
in a memo dated 01.09.1984 he handed over the possession of the 
holding Nos. 15, 16, 19, 24 and 28, Sultan Giash Uddin Road, 

<<PAGE 10>>
10 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 
Narayangonj belong to the JTC to the highest bidder Mamtaz Jute 
Belling Ltd.  
The documents relating to the transfer of the plots were 
exhibited as exhibit-II series. A tender notice was published on 
18.04.1981 to sell plot Nos. 15 and 19 by the BTC. Tempering the 
schedule of the said tender notice by different ink and handwriting 
holding No. 24 was inserted in the records and suppressing the fact 
as the Secretary of the Board, accused Maij Uddin fraudulently and 
mala fide obtained the approval of the 60th Board meeting of the JTC 
held on 28.03.1981 to sell plot No.24. No decision was taken by the 
Board to sell the holding Nos. 16 and 28. Subsequently, after the 
decision by the Board, the accused Maij Uddin, Enamul Muhit, Abul 
Hossein Chowdhury, Md. Motaleb and others in connivance with the 
Mamtaz Uddin, Proprietor of the M/s. Mamtaz Jute Belling Ltd, 
illegally executed deed No. 1657 dated 21.05.1991 and illegally 
handed over the possession of the plot Nos. 16, 24, 28. 
After handing over the possession of the said plots, the 
accused Abdul Hossein Chowdhury issued the letter of possession 
on 23.06.2005 although the holding Nos. 24 and 28 were not sold by 
the Board. The accused Lutfar Rahman by letter dated 01.09.1984 
directed the accused Abdul Hossein Chowdhury to hand over the 
possession of the plots to the M/S. Mamtaz Jute Belling Ltd. The 
accused Motaleb who is the billing assistant made a recommendation 
to initiate the file to hand over the possession.  
As regards the submission made by the learned Advocate 
regarding the non-examination of the informant and the 
Investigating Officer, it is found that the trial court by order dated 
18.03.2016 after perusal of the records arrived at the findings 

<<PAGE 11>>
11 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 
regarding the non-examination of the witnesses cited in the charge 
sheet that the prosecution case is based on the documentary evidence 
i.e. exhibit-II series. On perusal of the exhibit-II series as discussed 
herein above it transpires that the documentary evidence (exhibit-II 
series) proved by the prosecution is self-explanatory and during the 
trial of the case, the accused persons did not deny their signatures on 
the official documents i.e. exhibits-II series. During the trial, the 
informant and the investigating officer Musleh Uddin died. 
Therefore, there was no scope to examine the informant and the 
investigating officer, in the case. I am of the view that due to the 
non-examination of the informant and investigating officer, the 
defence was not prejudiced. 
It is found that the accused persons were serving with the Jute 
Corporation of Bangladesh and they were entrusted with the 
property of the Jute Corporation of Bangladesh but the accused 
persons in connivance with Mamtaz Uddin who was the owner of 
the M/S. Mamtaz Jute Belling Ltd by tempering the tender notice 
inserted Plot No. 24 in the records and suppressing the facts illegally 
sold Plot No. 24 to Mamataz Jute Belling Ltd. Although plots No. 16 
and 28 were not sold to Mamtaz Jute Belling Ltd, the accused 
persons fraudulently and malafide to misappropriate the plots 
illegally handed over the possession of plot Nos. 16 and 28 without 
any valid documents of sale. Thereby the accused persons 
committed offence under section 409 of the Penal Code read with 
section 5(2 )of the Prevention of Corruption Act, 1947.  
Considering the evidence adduced by the parties and the 
gravity of the offence, I am of the view that the ends of justice would 

<<PAGE 12>>
12 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 
be best served if the sentence passed by the trial court against the 
accused persons is modified as under: 
The accused Enamul Muhit, Abul Hossein Chowdhury, and 
Abdul Motalib are found guilty of the offence under section 409 of 
the Penal Code, 1860 read with section 5(2) of the Prevention of 
Corruption Act, 1947 and they are sentenced under section 409 of 
the Penal Code, 1860 to suffer rigorous imprisonment for 2 (two) 
years and fine of Tk. 49,08,750. The order of the trial court as 
regards the confiscation of plot Nos. 16, 24 and 28 in favour of the 
state is affirmed by this court.  
The Criminal Appeal No. 12765 of 2018 so far relates to 
judgment and order of conviction of appellant Maij Uddin is abated. 
The appellant Maij Uddin is sentenced to pay a fine of Tk. 49,08,750 
which is recoverable following law. 
The Criminal Appeal No. 12765 of 2008 so far relates to 
accused Enamul Muhit and Abul Hossein Chowdhury and Criminal 
Appeal No. 4915 of 2018 are disposed of with modification of 
sentence.  
The appellants Enamul Muhit, Abul Hossain Chowdhury and 
Abdul Motalib are directed to surrender before the trial court 
forthwith.  
The trial Court is directed to do the needful.   
Send down the LCR at once.
input_summary: APPELLANTs are four persons who stood trial before a special judge on allegations that they misappropriated the sale proceeds of surplus plots of a state-owned jute corporation by transferring those plots to private persons on the strength of a manipulated tender notice. The STATE is the respondent. The appellants seek acquittal from the conviction and from the sentences of imprisonment, fine and confiscation imposed on them. Their grounds are that entrustment and dishonest intention were not proved, that the trial examined only a handful of witnesses, that the tampering was never traced to them and that the fine cannot subsist after the death of one appellant.
explanation: The court held that the documentary material established entrustment of the corporation's plots to the appellants and their dishonest transfer of those plots to private buyers, so the finding of criminal breach of trust read with the anti-corruption provision was maintained so far as the three surviving appellants were concerned. The appeal of the appellant who had died during the pendency was declared to have abated, though the fine already imposed remained recoverable from his estate. The imprisonment was reduced to two years, while the fine and the confiscation of the three plots were affirmed. The small number of witnesses examined at trial was held not to weaken the documentary proof.

input_summary: APPELLANT is a stenographer of a divisional office who was tried on allegations of criminal breach of trust and forgery for procuring, on the strength of a forged allotment letter and a forged letter of authority, the release of forms worth nearly fifty thousand taka to a person who was not entitled to them. The STATE is the respondent. He seeks acquittal from the conviction and sentence passed by the special judge. His grounds are that the letter of authority said to bear his signature was never sent to the handwriting expert, that the letters were never proved to have been posted at all, and that he merely carried out clerical duties at the instance of his superiors.
explanation: The court found that the appellant's alleged signature on the letter of authority had never been examined by the handwriting expert, and that attestation of a mere photograph of the document could not fill that gap. Nothing on record proved that the two letters had actually been posted, nor that the appellant had handled the transaction at any stage. Since he was only a stenographer acting under the instructions of others, the court regarded him as a scapegoat and held the charge unproved beyond reasonable doubt. The conviction and sentence were consequently reversed and the appeal succeeded.

The petitioners seek a declaration that the notice listing allottees and the tender notice for allocation of the spaces as parking are without lawful authority, and a direction that the respective shops be allotted to them on payment of rent, salami and taxes. Their grounds are that they built the shops at their own cost under allotment letters, that those shops were pulled down without notice, and that the corporation acted against the municipal statute, the market rules and natural justice while defeating their legitimate expectation.
explanation: The court found the demolition of the petitioners' shops by the corporation without any notice to be wholly without lawful authority. The respondents had shown no prejudice if the spaces were allotted to the petitioners, who had raised the construction with their own money under the corporation's approval, had carried on business there for about twenty-five years and had acquired goodwill and a legitimate expectation of allotment. Observing that no objection had been taken against them and that justice would be better served by regularising their holding, the court directed that permanent allotment be made in their favour on payment of salami as per the corporation's rules.

However, the provision of the three essentials of a gift as 
mentioned in Article No.149 of the D.F Mulla’s Mahomedan Law, 
wherein, the three conditions have been disclosed that: 
“It is essential to the validity of a gift that there should be 
(1) a declaration of gift by the donor, 
 (2) an acceptance of the gift, express or implied, by or on 
behalf of the donee, and  
(3) delivery of possession of the subject of the gift by the 
donor to the donee as mentioned in Section-150.”                                  
And Article 150 states that:  
“(1) It is essential to the validity of a gift that there should 
be a delivery of such possession as the subject of the gift is 
susceptible of (1). As observed by the Judicial Committee, 
"the taking of possession of the subject-matter of the gift 
by the donee, either actually or constructively," is 
necessary to complete a gift.”

<<PAGE 11>>

11
And sub-article 2 of article 150 specifically states the procedure 
of the registration of a deed of gift does not cure the want of delivery 
of possession.  
And in the Article 152 of D.F Mulla’s Mahomedan Law 
specifically mentions that:  
“A gift of immovable property of which the donor is in 
actual possession is not complete, unless the donor 
physically departs from the premises with all his goods 
and chattels, and the done formally enters into 
possession.”  
And in the Article 167 of D.F Mulla’s Mahomedan Law describes 
the provision of revocation of gifts as follows:  
“(1) A gift may be revoked by the donor at any time before 
delivery of possession. The reason is that before delivery 
there is no completed gift at all. 
(2) Subject to the provisions of sub-sec. (4), a gift may be 
revoked even after delivery of possession except in the 
following cases- 
(a) when the gift is made by a husband to his wife or by 
wife to her husband; 
(b) when the donee is related to the donor within the 
prohibited degrees; 
(c) when the donee is dead;

<<PAGE 12>>

12
(d) when the thing given has passed out of the donee's 
possession by sale (e), gift or otherwise; 
(e) when the thing given is lost or destroyed; 
(f) when the thing given has increased in value, whatever 
be the cause of the increase; 
(g) when the thing given is so changed that it cannot be 
identified, as when wheat is converted into flour by 
grinding;  
(h) when the donor has received something in exchange 
(iwaz) for the gift.”  
The original donor is the father of the either side and 
accordingly he had desired to gift the suit property in faovur of his six 
sons and one daughter equally and accordingly he vested the power to 
his one son, the defendant-petitioner No.1, but upon obtaining the 
certified copy, the donor found that the intentions were not 
accordingly reflected in the deed thus immediately after knowing the 
said facts, he filed the suit for cancellation of the said gift deed. 
It appears that the plaintiff also deposed before the Court and 
categorically stated the said the facts and the P.W-3 also supported 
the said deposition of P.W-1. Considering the entire provisions of law 
and the facts and circumstances of the case, it appears that the donor 
expressed his intention to gift the land in favour of his six sons and 
one daughter equally and accordingly vested the power to the

<<PAGE 13>>

13
defendant-petitioner No.1 but ultimately the defendant petitioner

suit and the provisions of law, it is my view that the Appellate Court 
rightly passed the impugned judgment and did not commit any error 
in law resulting in an error in the decision occasioning failure of 
justice.  
Therefore, the Appellate Court passed a decree of partition, and 
accordingly Advocate Commissioner was appointed and the Advocate 
Commissioner physically delivered the possession to the opposite 
parties and accordingly final decree was drawn up, but the petitioner

However, it is my considered view that the gift deed executed 
by the original plaintiff was obtained against his will and accordingly I 
do not find any merit in the Rule.  
In the result, the Rule is discharged without any order as to cost. 
The impugned judgment and decree dated 28.03.2022 (decree signed

<<PAGE 14>>

14
on 03.04.2022) passed by the learned Special Judge, Faridpur, in Other 
Class Appeal No.70 of 2016, allowing the appeal and thereby reversing 
the judgment and decree dated 08.03.2016 (decree signed on 
19.04.2016) passed by the learned Senior Assistant Judge, Fridpur in 
Other Class Suit No.78 of 2010 is hereby upheld.

input_summary: PETITIONERs are the defendants in a suit brought by the heirs of a deceased father for cancellation of a registered deed of gift which he had executed in favour of some of his sons. The OPPOSITE PARTY is the plaintiff side. The petitioners challenge the appellate judgment which reversed the trial court's decree and decreed the suit. Their grounds are that the deed was duly registered and could not be cancelled, that the defendants never contested the suit and that no breach of the deed's terms was shown, and that a registered instrument stands until a competent civil court cancels it. The opposite party say the deed was obtained by fraud, excluding three sons, and that possession never passed.
explanation: The court applied the essentials of a valid gift under Muslim law, namely declaration, acceptance and delivery of possession, and held that registration alone does not cure the want of possession. On the evidence, the father's intention was to give his land equally to his six sons and one daughter, yet the deed confined the benefit to some of them, and the donor never physically parted with possession. The plaintiff had deposed to that effect and his witness supported him. The court therefore found the deed to have been obtained against the donor's will and no error in the appellate decision, particularly as the final decree had gone unchallenged.

on

and

Judgment on 10.07.2024 
 
 
This Rule is directed against the judgment and decree dated 
01.01.2020 passed by the learned Additional District Judge, 3rd 
Court, Khulna, in Family Appeal No.62 of 2016, allowing in part and 
thereby modifying the judgment and decree dated 09.05.2016 
passed by the learned Assistant Judge, Family Court (Rupsha), 
Khulna, in Family Suit No.671 of 2011.  
The facts necessary for the disposal of the Rule are that the 
opposite party, No. 1, as plaintiff, instituted a family suit bearing No. 
671 of 201 before Family Court Khulna for money decree towards 

<<PAGE 2>>
 
2
 
prompt dower and for Maintenance of plaintiff NO.1-2 contending, 
inter-alia that on 24.09.2009 the plaintiff No.1 was married to the 
defendant through a registered kabinnama fixing dower at 
Tk.2,00,001/-; that in their conjugal life, a daughter was born out of 
their wedlock; that after the birth of the child defendant started to 
torture the plaintiff No.1 in demand of dowry; that on 05.04.2011 the 
defendant called her father and sister over the phone giving 
information about her sickness; the defendant forcefully took 
signatures of plaintiff No.1 and her father and sister and also took 
L.T.I. of the plaintiff No.1 on some papers and stamps and created 
forged Talaqnama using those signatures; after taking their 
signatures defendant took plaintiff No.1 and her father and sister to 
Mawferryghat and then boarded them at launch; the plaintiff No.1 
did not divorce defendant; she has been living in her father’s house 
since 07.04.2011; on 21.10.2011 the plaintiff demanded dower and 
Maintenance from the defendant over the phone but he refused to 
pay; hence the suit. 
On the other hand, the defendant-petitioner contested the suit 
by filing a written statement denying all the material allegations 
brought in the plaint. The defendant’s case is that during their 
conjugal life after a daughter was born, plaintiff No.1 tortured her 
physically and mentally; on 29.03.2011, the father and sister of 
plaintiff No.1 came to her house and at the mediation of local 
respectable people and the father and sister of the plaintiff No.1 has 

<<PAGE 3>>
 
3
 
been dissolved by way of khula talaq on 30.03.2011 which had been 
registered in the office of Notary Public and the office of Marriage 
and Divorce Register; the plaintiff No.1 received Tk.2,00,001/- as 
dower and Tk.1,30,000/- as Maintenance of plaintiff No.2. So they 
are not entitled to get any dower and Maintenance. With this 
averments, he prayed for dismissal of the suit. 
Upon the pleadings of both the parties, the learned Assistant 
Judge and Family Court framed three issues in the suit. 
Both the parties adduced and produced evidence in support of 
their respective cases. 
Consequently, the learned Assistant Judge, Family Court 
(Rupsha), Khulna, dismissed the suit by the judgment and decree 
dated 09.05.2016. 
Being aggrieved by and dissatisfied with the above judgment 
and decree, the plaintiff, as appellant, preferred Family Appeal 
No.62 of 2016 before District Judge Khulna. On transfer, the appeal 
was heard by the learned Additional District Judge, 3rd Court, 
Khulna. Eventually, the learned Additional District Judge, 3rd Court, 
Khulna, by the judgment and decree dated 01.01.2020, partly 
allowed the appeal. 
Being aggrieved by and dissatisfied with the impugned 
judgment and decree dated 01.01.2020, the defendant-petitioner 
preferred the present Civil Revision and obtained the instant Rule 
and an order of stay. 

<<PAGE 4>>
 
4
 
Mr. Nahid Hossain, the learned Advocate appearing on behalf 
of the defendant-petitioner, submits that the appellate court below 
failed to consider that the plaintiff is not entitled to get her dower 
money and Maintenance as she has already received Tk.2,00,001/- 
and 1,13,000/- from the defendant petitioner as dower and 
Maintenance, so the appellate court below committed an error of 
Law resulting in an error in the decision an occasioning failure of 
justice; that the appellate court below failed to consider that the trial 
court rightly arrived a correct decision that the divorce was 
accomplished by both the consenting parties with the consent of the 
husband and the wife. 
 Mr. Md. Shahidul Islam, the learned Counsel appearing for 
the opposite party No.1, submits that the Judgment and Decree of 
the appellate court were proper, but the family court did not at all 
consider the existing Law of the country, had arbitrarily rejected the 
suit.  
I have considered the submission of the learned Counsel for 
both parties. perused the impugned judgment and decree of the 
courts below and other material available on record. 
Admittedly, plaintiff No.2 is the daughter of the defendant. 
Admittedly, the defendant had paid Taka 5000/- monthly from 
23.05.2911 to 14.97.2011 to defendant No. 2. 
To substantiate the submissions advanced by the Bar, the 
relevant Law may be quoted as follows:-- 

<<PAGE 5>>
 
5
 
 “370. Maintenance of children and grandchildren--- (1) A 
father is bound to maintain his sons until they have attained 
the age of puberty. He is also bound to maintain his daughters 
until they are married. But he is not bound to maintain his 
adult sons unless they are disabled by infirmity or disease. The 
fact that the children are in the custody of their mother during 
their infancy does not relieve the father from the obligation of 
maintaining them. But the father is not bound to maintain a 
child who is capable of being maintained out of his or her own 
property. 
(2) if the father is poor and incapable of his own labour, the 
mother,  if she is in easy circumstances, is bound   
to maintain her children as the father would be. 
3. If the father is poor and infirm, and the mother also is  poor, 
the oblegation to maintain the children lies on the 
grandfather, provided he is in easy circumstances.’’  
It manifests that a father must provide Maintenance to his 
unmarried daughter until married as per the provision 
enumerated in section 370 of the Mohammadan Law.  
In view of the above, I am of the view that the defendant 
petitioner is bound to maintain his unmarried daughter( plaintiff 
No.2) till the date of her marital status. The law does not say that the 
daughter will lose her right to maintenance from her father after 
attending the age of eighteen (18). 

<<PAGE 6>>
 
6
 
It is revealed that the court of appeal below, having considered 
the evidence of P.Ws. and D.Ws., rightly allowed the appeal by 
modifying the judgment and decree of the trial Court. Therefore, I 
find no reason to take a view different from that of the learned 
Additional District Judge, 3rd Court, Khulna. Since the plaintiff-
opposite party has been living in a different residence since 
15.07.2011 without receiving any maintenance cost from the 
defendant, the court of appeal below rightly allowed maintenance 
costs in favour of the plaintiff-daughter with effect from 15.07.2011 
which is very much reasonable in the facts and circumstances of the 
case. 
The 
appellate 
court 
below 
allowed 
the 
amount 
of 
Tk.3,00,000/- to be given for past Maintenance for his daughter and 
Tk.3,000/- per month for the running time for his daughter, i.e., 
opposite party No.2 and Tk.100 will be increased every calendar 
year. We allow the same and find no merit in the Rule. 
Resultantly, the Rule is discharged without any order as to 
cost.  
The impugned judgment and decree dated 01.01.2020 passed 
by the learned Additional District Judge, 3rd Court, Khulna, in 
Family Appeal No.62 of 2016 is hereby affirmed. 
Send down the L.C. records and communicate this judgment. 
 
……………………. 
  (Md. Salim, J).

explanation: The court held that a father is bound to maintain his unmarried daughter until she is married, and that Muslim law fixes no age at which that right comes to an end. The court consequently saw no reason to take a view different from that of the Additional District Judge, who had fixed a lump sum for past maintenance and a monthly allowance with an annual increase for the daughter, and confirmed those terms. The revision was found to be without merit.

IN THE SUPREME COURT OF BANGLADESH 
HIGH COURT DIVISION 
(CIVIL REVISIONAL JURISDICTION) 
Present: 
 
     MR. JUSTICE S.M. EMDADUL HOQUE
